problems.e: Exhaustive simulation needs $2^{64}$ vectors, but an equivalence checker proves the structure equals the language's adder for all inputs.

problems.q:
Random simulation of a generated 16-bit signed saturating adder passes a million vectors. What should still worry you?

A) The adder must be wrong since it passed so quickly

B) Random tests always miss overflow

C) Nothing, a million vectors is exhaustive for 16 bits

D) Rare corner cases such as the most negative value may not have been hit
problems.a: Rare corner cases such as the most negative value may not have been hit
problems.e: Two 16-bit operands give about four billion pairs; a million random ones sample a small fraction, so corners need directed tests or a formal check.

problems.q:
An agent writes a 12-input combinational decoder. Which golden check gives complete assurance at low cost?

A) A thousand random vectors

B) Exhaustive simulation of all 4096 input combinations against a reference

C) Reviewing the RTL for style

D) Checking that synthesis area is small
problems.a: Exhaustive simulation of all 4096 input combinations against a reference
problems.e: Twelve inputs give 4096 rows, cheap to enumerate, so the check covers every case.

problems.q:
The model writes both the RTL and the testbench that checks it. What is the weakness?

A) Both can share the same misunderstanding, so the test passes a wrong design

B) Lint cannot check testbench code

C) Testbenches cannot be generated by models

D) The simulation will run too slowly
problems.a: Both can share the same misunderstanding, so the test passes a wrong design
problems.e: A golden reference must be independent of the generated design, or a shared mistake goes undetected.

problems.q:
The model writes both the RTL and the testbench that checks it. What is the weakness?

A) Testbenches cannot be generated by models

B) Lint cannot check testbench code

C) The simulation will run too slowly

D) Both can share the same misunderstanding, so the test passes a wrong design
problems.a: Both can share the same misunderstanding, so the test passes a wrong design
problems.e: A golden reference must be independent of the generated design, or a shared mistake goes undetected.

problems.q:
A confirmed spec decision (reset value, signedness) should be kept where?

A) Only in the model's conversation context

B) Nowhere; each request should start fresh

C) In a recorded specification the next request starts from

D) In a comment inside the generated RTL alone
problems.a: In a recorded specification the next request starts from
problems.e: Recording decisions avoids re-asking and keeps later generated blocks consistent.

label: Golden and differential checks for generated RTL
lesson:
# Golden and differential checks for generated RTL

When an agent changes RTL, two questions need evidence: is the new design correct against the specification (golden), and did it change only what was intended (differential)? Digital logic offers unusually sharp instruments for both: combinational and sequential equivalence checking, exhaustive simulation for small blocks, and QoR comparisons after synthesis. Knowing what each instrument proves is the difference between a trusted agent and a plausible one.

## What each check proves

- **Directed or random simulation** shows the design behaves correctly on the vectors run, and nothing about the rest. Exhaustive simulation of an $n$-input combinational block needs $2^n$ vectors: fine at 16 inputs, hopeless at 64.
- **Combinational equivalence checking** proves that two netlists with matching registers compute the same next-state and output functions for every input, using SAT and structural hashing. It is the standard check after synthesis.
- **Sequential equivalence checking** proves two designs produce the same outputs from reset for every input sequence, even when their registers differ (retiming, re-encoded FSMs).
- **Property checking** proves stated properties hold, which is only as strong as the properties.

## Differential checks for an edit

For a refactoring edit (re-encoding an FSM, replacing a ripple adder by a prefix adder, retiming a pipeline) the right check is equivalence against the previous version: behavior must not change at all. For a functional edit (add a saturate mode, change a reset value) equivalence must fail, and the check becomes: equivalent under the old mode, and the new behavior matches the specification under the new one. Constrain the comparison to the unchanged modes and prove those equivalent.

On top of correctness, a differential QoR report after synthesis (area, worst slack, cell count, power estimate) shows whether the edit had the intended physical effect, and nothing else moved.

## Pitfalls

Equivalence checkers need a correspondence or a reset state, and both can hide problems. Two FSMs equivalent from reset can differ from an illegal state, which matters if the specification requires safe recovery. A design that is equivalent only because both versions share the same bug (both copied from one wrong reference) passes every differential check; that is why the golden reference must be independent.

Don't-care handling is another trap: synthesis may exploit X assignments differently in the two versions, so an equivalence check that treats X as a free choice can pass designs that simulate differently. A trustworthy harness states its X semantics and its reset assumptions alongside every pass.

## Going deeper

Kuehlmann and Krohm, "Equivalence Checking Using Cuts and Heaps" (DAC, 1997); Mishchenko et al., "Improvements to Combinational Equivalence Checking" (ICCAD, 2006); the ABC documentation for cec and dsec.

problems.q:
How many vectors does exhaustive simulation of a 20-input combinational block need?

A) About one million

B) About one billion

C) About 400

D) About one thousand
problems.a: About one million
problems.e: $2^{20} = 1048576$ input combinations.

problems.q:
A retimed pipeline moved registers across logic. Which check can prove it still matches the original?

A) Lint

B) Combinational equivalence with name matching

C) Sequential equivalence checking

D) A static timing report
problems.a: Sequential equivalence checking
problems.e: Retiming breaks register correspondence, so equivalence must be proved over sequences from reset.

problems.q:
Two netlists have the same registers, matched by name. Which check proves they compute the same functions?

A) Random simulation

B) Sequential equivalence checking from reset

C) A QoR comparison

D) Combinational equivalence checking
problems.a: Combinational equivalence checking
problems.e: With corresponding registers, equivalence reduces to proving every next-state and output function equal, a combinational problem.

problems.q:
A change was meant to affect only the multiplier, yet the differential QoR shows the control FSM's area changed too. What is the right reaction?

A) Accept it, since total area went down

B) Revert the multiplier change only

C) Investigate: the edit had an unintended effect outside its target

D) Ignore it as synthesis noise in all cases
problems.a: Investigate: the edit had an unintended effect outside its target
problems.e: Differential checks exist to show that only the intended part moved; an unexpected change needs an explanation.

problems.q:
An agent replaces a ripple adder with a Brent-Kung adder as a pure refactor. What must the differential check show?

A) Only that the new design synthesizes

B) That the testbench still compiles

C) That some outputs changed, proving the edit took effect

D) Full equivalence with the previous version, plus the intended QoR change
problems.a: Full equivalence with the previous version, plus the intended QoR change
problems.e: A refactor must not change behavior at all, and the QoR diff shows the intended timing and area effect.

problems.q:
A change was meant to affect only the multiplier, yet the differential QoR shows the control FSM's area changed too. What is the right reaction?

A) Ignore it as synthesis noise in all cases

B) Investigate: the edit had an unintended effect outside its target

C) Accept it, since total area went down

D) Revert the multiplier change only
problems.a: Investigate: the edit had an unintended effect outside its target
problems.e: Differential checks exist to show that only the intended part moved; an unexpected change needs an explanation.

problems.q:
Synthesis is free to choose values for X assignments. Why can that make an equivalence pass misleading?

A) X values are always resolved to 0 by every tool

B) The two versions may resolve X differently and simulate differently, while the checker treats X as a free choice

C) X assignments are illegal in synthesizable RTL

D) Equivalence checkers reject any design containing X
problems.a: The two versions may resolve X differently and simulate differently, while the checker treats X as a free choice
problems.e: The X semantics of the check must be stated, or a pass may hide behavior differences that simulation would show.

problems.q:
What should a trustworthy harness report alongside every equivalence pass?

A) Only the runtime of the check

B) The number of lines changed

C) Its reset assumptions and its treatment of X and don't-cares

D) The model's confidence score
problems.a: Its reset assumptions and its treatment of X and don't-cares
problems.e: Those assumptions define what the proof covers; without them a reviewer cannot judge its strength.

problems.q:
Both the old and new versions of a block were derived from the same flawed reference model. What will the differential check show?

A) A QoR regression

B) A pass, because both share the same bug

C) A failure at the bug's location

D) A lint error
problems.a: A pass, because both share the same bug
problems.e: Differential checks prove sameness, not correctness; an independent golden reference is needed to catch a shared bug.

label: Agent design-space exploration of arithmetic
prereqs: Fast and accurate engines in a modeling loop
lesson:
# Agent design-space exploration of arithmetic

Adders and multipliers have a rich, well-understood architecture space: ripple, carry-select, Sklansky, Brent-Kung, Kogge-Stone and hybrids for addition; array, Booth, Wallace, Dadda and compressor trees for multiplication. An agent exploring that space for a given width and timing target is a natural fast-and-accurate loop: analytic models prune, synthesis and placement decide. This concept is about running that loop correctly.

## Fast filters from closed forms

The closed forms from this domain are a fast model. For an $n$-bit adder: ripple has depth $n$ carry steps and $n$ cells; Brent-Kung $2\log_2 n - 1$ levels and $2n - 2 - \log_2 n$ nodes; Sklansky $\log_2 n$ levels and $\frac{n}{2}\log_2 n$ nodes with fanout $n/2$; Kogge-Stone $\log_2 n$ levels and $n\log_2 n - n + 1$ nodes. Given a delay per level and a budget, an agent can discard every architecture that cannot possibly meet timing and rank the survivors by node count, in microseconds.

The cheapest candidate that meets the budget on this model is the starting point, not the answer, because the model ignores wires, fanout loading and placement.

## Recursing to the accurate engines

The accurate evaluation is synthesis, placement and timing on the real library. It is expensive, so the agent spends it on the frontier: the few candidates within the fast model's error margin of each other, or of the budget. Kogge-Stone looks best on depth, but its long wires and high node count often lose to Sklansky or Han-Carlson once placed; Brent-Kung looks worst on depth but may meet a loose target at half the area.

The loop should record each fast-model estimate next to its accurate result. The gap between them, per architecture and width, calibrates the fast model, and a systematic gap (Kogge-Stone always slower than predicted) is exactly the knowledge worth keeping.

## Objectives and traps

The objective must match what the design needs: minimum area subject to timing, or minimum delay subject to area, or energy per operation at a throughput. An agent optimizing a single scalar (say area plus a weighted delay) may land on a point that violates a hard constraint the weight did not capture. Pareto fronts are safer: keep every candidate not dominated on (delay, area, power).

Two traps recur. Synthesis tools already choose adder architectures internally, so an explicit architecture in RTL may be re-optimized away; the agent must check what was actually built. And a comparison at one corner or one width does not transfer: the winner at 16 bits is often not the winner at 64.

## Going deeper

Harris, "A Taxonomy of Parallel Prefix Networks" (Asilomar, 2003); Zimmermann, "Binary Adder Architectures for Cell-Based VLSI and their Synthesis" (1997); Roy et al., "PrefixRL: Optimization of Parallel Prefix Circuits using Deep Reinforcement Learning" (DAC, 2021).

problems.q:
An agent explores 32-bit adder architectures. Its fast model treats each level as 40 ps and uses: ripple-carry, 32 levels and 32 nodes; Brent-Kung, $2\log_2 n - 1$ levels and $2n - 2 - \log_2 n$ nodes, fanout 2; Sklansky, $\log_2 n$ levels and $\frac{n}{2}\log_2 n$ nodes, fanout $n/2$; Kogge-Stone, $\log_2 n$ levels and $n\log_2 n - n + 1$ nodes, fanout 2. The budget is 200 ps and the library allows a fanout of at most 64. Which architecture should it send to synthesis first, as the cheapest candidate meeting both limits?

A) Ripple-carry

B) Sklansky

C) Kogge-Stone

D) Brent-Kung
problems.a: Sklansky
problems.e: At n = 32 the candidates have (levels, nodes, fanout) of ripple (32, 32, 2), Brent-Kung (9, 57, 2), Sklansky (5, 80, 16), Kogge-Stone (5, 129, 2). The depth budget allows 5 levels; the cheapest feasible one is Sklansky with 80 nodes.

problems.q:
An agent explores 64-bit adder architectures. Its fast model treats each level as 20 ps and uses: ripple-carry, 64 levels and 64 nodes; Brent-Kung, $2\log_2 n - 1$ levels and $2n - 2 - \log_2 n$ nodes, fanout 2; Sklansky, $\log_2 n$ levels and $\frac{n}{2}\log_2 n$ nodes, fanout $n/2$; Kogge-Stone, $\log_2 n$ levels and $n\log_2 n - n + 1$ nodes, fanout 2. The budget is 160 ps and the library allows a fanout of at most 8. Which architecture should it send to synthesis first, as the cheapest candidate meeting both limits?

A) Ripple-carry

B) Kogge-Stone

C) Sklansky

D) Brent-Kung
problems.a: Kogge-Stone
problems.e: At n = 64 the candidates have (levels, nodes, fanout) of ripple (64, 64, 2), Brent-Kung (11, 120, 2), Sklansky (6, 192, 32), Kogge-Stone (6, 321, 2). The depth budget allows 8 levels; the cheapest feasible one is Kogge-Stone with 321 nodes.

problems.q:
An agent explores 16-bit adder architectures. Its fast model treats each level as 35 ps and uses: ripple-carry, 16 levels and 16 nodes; Brent-Kung, $2\log_2 n - 1$ levels and $2n - 2 - \log_2 n$ nodes, fanout 2; Sklansky, $\log_2 n$ levels and $\frac{n}{2}\log_2 n$ nodes, fanout $n/2$; Kogge-Stone, $\log_2 n$ levels and $n\log_2 n - n + 1$ nodes, fanout 2. The budget is 280 ps and the library allows a fanout of at most 64. Which architecture should it send to synthesis first, as the cheapest candidate meeting both limits?

A) Sklansky

B) Kogge-Stone

C) Brent-Kung

D) Ripple-carry
problems.a: Brent-Kung
problems.e: At n = 16 the candidates have (levels, nodes, fanout) of ripple (16, 16, 2), Brent-Kung (7, 26, 2), Sklansky (4, 32, 8), Kogge-Stone (4, 49, 2). The depth budget allows 8 levels; the cheapest feasible one is Brent-Kung with 26 nodes.

problems.q:
Which split of work matches the fast-and-accurate loop for arithmetic exploration?

A) Closed forms only, with no accurate runs

B) Closed forms and quick synthesis rank candidates; placement and timing decide among the finalists

C) Accurate runs only, with no fast model

D) Placement and timing for every candidate, closed forms for the finalist
problems.a: Closed forms and quick synthesis rank candidates; placement and timing decide among the finalists
problems.e: Cheap models cover the space broadly; expensive engines are reserved for the frontier.

problems.q:
The agent records fast estimates beside post-synthesis results and finds Kogge-Stone is consistently 15% slower than predicted. What should it do?

A) Report the fast estimate as the result

B) Stop using the fast model altogether

C) Discard the synthesis results as noise

D) Calibrate the fast model with a correction for that architecture
problems.a: Calibrate the fast model with a correction for that architecture
problems.e: A systematic gap is knowledge: it improves the fast model for the next exploration.

problems.q:
A post-synthesis result for a candidate is within 2 ps of the budget. What is the right next step?

A) Recurse to placement and routing before trusting it, since wires can push it over

B) Reject it immediately

C) Rerun the closed-form model

D) Accept it, since synthesis is signoff
problems.a: Recurse to placement and routing before trusting it, since wires can push it over
problems.e: Near the budget, only the more accurate engine can settle feasibility.

problems.q:
Why keep a Pareto set of (delay, area, power) rather than a single best design?

A) It avoids running synthesis

B) Different contexts need different trade-offs, and dominated points can be dropped safely

C) A Pareto set always contains exactly one design

D) It guarantees the fastest design is also smallest
problems.a: Different contexts need different trade-offs, and dominated points can be dropped safely
problems.e: The Pareto set keeps every non-dominated option, so a later constraint picks from it without re-exploring.

problems.q:
The best adder at 16 bits is reused without re-exploration for a 64-bit datapath. Why is that risky?

A) The 16-bit design will not synthesize at 64 bits

B) 64-bit adders cannot use prefix networks

C) Depth, node and wire costs scale differently, so the ranking can change with width

D) Width does not affect the choice at all
problems.a: Depth, node and wire costs scale differently, so the ranking can change with width
problems.e: Ripple delay grows linearly while prefix depth grows logarithmically, and wire costs grow with width, so winners change.

problems.q:
The best adder at 16 bits is reused without re-exploration for a 64-bit datapath. Why is that risky?

A) Width does not affect the choice at all

B) The 16-bit design will not synthesize at 64 bits

C) 64-bit adders cannot use prefix networks

D) Depth, node and wire costs scale differently, so the ranking can change with width
problems.a: Depth, node and wire costs scale differently, so the ranking can change with width
problems.e: Ripple delay grows linearly while prefix depth grows logarithmically, and wire costs grow with width, so winners change.

label: Change tiers for parameterized RTL generators
lesson:
# Change tiers for parameterized RTL generators

Much RTL is not written by hand but generated: parameterized modules, Chisel or other hardware-construction-language generators, memory compilers, arithmetic generators. A generator is an engine in the four-layer sense, with a core (the elaboration framework and its invariants), policies (architectures), parameters (widths, depths) and hooks. Placing each change request at the right tier is what keeps agent edits safe.

## Tier 1: parameters

Most requests to a generator are parameter changes: data width, FIFO depth, number of pipeline stages, number of read ports, column-mux factor of a memory, an option to register the outputs. These need no code change: the generator is re-run with new values, and the existing golden tests (parameterized to match) re-verify the result.

A well-designed generator exposes these explicitly and validates them (depth a power of two, width at least 1) so that a configuration change cannot produce an illegal design. An agent that edits generator source to change a width is working at the wrong tier.

## Tier 2: a new policy at a seam

Adding a new adder architecture to an arithmetic generator, a new FSM encoding to a controller generator, or a new replacement policy to a cache generator is a plug-in change. The seam is an interface: for an adder generator, "given $n$ and the $(g, p)$ signals, return a prefix network", with the generate-propagate logic and the sum XORs staying in the core. The new policy (say a Han-Carlson network) implements only the prefix network.

The proof is differential: the new architecture must be combinationally equivalent to the existing ones at every width tested, and its QoR report shows where it sits on the depth-area trade-off.

## Tier 3: the core

Core changes alter the generator's invariants or framework: how clocks and resets are emitted, how modules are named and connected, the intermediate representation, the semantics of a parameter. They can affect every design the generator has ever produced, so they need a human-approved diff and full regression across all configurations.

Some requests look small but are core: "make all generated flip-flops use asynchronous reset" changes reset semantics everywhere and interacts with timing and CDC checks. The tier is set by what the change can affect, not by how many lines it touches.

## Going deeper

Bachrach et al., "Chisel: Constructing Hardware in a Scala Embedded Language" (DAC, 2012); Shacham et al., "Rethinking Digital Design: Why Design Must Change" (IEEE Micro, 2010).

problems.q:
An agent edits the generator's source to change a data width from 32 to 48. What is wrong?

A) Widths cannot be changed at all

B) Nothing, source edits are always preferred

C) It should edit the netlist instead

D) It is working at the wrong tier: width should be a validated parameter
problems.a: It is working at the wrong tier: width should be a validated parameter
problems.e: Parameter changes belong at tier 1 so they need no code change and no recompile.

problems.q:
A team asks for one more pipeline stage in a generated multiplier that already exposes a stage count. Which tier?

A) It cannot be done with a generator

B) Tier 2, plug-in

C) Tier 1, configuration

D) Tier 3, core
problems.a: Tier 1, configuration
problems.e: When the stage count is a parameter, adding a stage is a configuration change.

problems.q:
Why should a generator validate parameter values before elaboration?

A) So the core never needs testing

B) So a configuration change cannot produce an illegal design

C) So parameters can be ignored

D) So it runs faster
problems.a: So a configuration change cannot produce an illegal design
problems.e: Validation keeps tier 1 safe: a bad value is rejected rather than turned into broken RTL.

problems.q:
A plug-in replacement policy for a cache generator passes its tests. What must remain untouched?

A) The golden tests

B) The QoR baseline

C) The cache's data array size parameter

D) The generator core, including tag comparison and the interface to the policy
problems.a: The generator core, including tag comparison and the interface to the policy
problems.e: Tier 2 changes live behind the seam; the core and its contracts stay fixed.

problems.q:
A plug-in replacement policy for a cache generator passes its tests. What must remain untouched?

A) The cache's data array size parameter

B) The golden tests

C) The generator core, including tag comparison and the interface to the policy

D) The QoR baseline
problems.a: The generator core, including tag comparison and the interface to the policy
problems.e: Tier 2 changes live behind the seam; the core and its contracts stay fixed.

problems.q:
What should the seam for adder architectures in an arithmetic generator take and return?

A) Take the width and the g, p signals; return a prefix network producing the group generates

B) Take the whole RTL module and return a netlist

C) Take the clock period and return a gate count

D) Take the sum bits and return the carries
problems.a: Take the width and the g, p signals; return a prefix network producing the group generates
problems.e: A narrow interface keeps the shared logic in the core and lets each policy supply only the prefix network.

problems.q:
Requests for one kind of change keep landing in tier 3. What does that indicate?

A) Agents should not handle such requests

B) The tier model does not apply to generators

C) The core is well designed

D) A missing seam: the variable behavior should be moved behind an extension point
problems.a: A missing seam: the variable behavior should be moved behind an extension point
problems.e: A seam is in the right place when that kind of change essentially never needs a core edit.

problems.q:
Requests for one kind of change keep landing in tier 3. What does that indicate?

A) Agents should not handle such requests

B) The core is well designed

C) The tier model does not apply to generators

D) A missing seam: the variable behavior should be moved behind an extension point
problems.a: A missing seam: the variable behavior should be moved behind an extension point
problems.e: A seam is in the right place when that kind of change essentially never needs a core edit.

problems.q:
What does a tier 3 change to a generator require before it is merged?

A) Only a passing compile

B) Nothing beyond the agent's review

C) A single golden test

D) A human-approved diff and full regression across configurations
problems.a: A human-approved diff and full regression across configurations
problems.e: Core changes can affect every design the generator produces.

label: Tool-grounded rewards for RTL agents
prereqs: Golden and differential checks for generated RTL
lesson:
# Tool-grounded rewards for RTL agents

Training or tuning a model to write RTL needs a reward, and the natural one is tool-grounded: compile it, test it, prove it, synthesize it, and score the outcome. Each tool gives a different signal at a different cost and with a different exploit. Designing the reward is the hard part, because a model optimizes exactly what is measured.

## Building the reward from tools

A layered reward for generated RTL: zero unless it parses and elaborates; partial credit for passing lint; most of the credit for passing functional checks (test bench, then formal equivalence or properties); and a QoR term (area, delay, power after synthesis) only for designs that are already correct. Gating QoR on correctness matters: otherwise the cheapest design, one that does nothing, scores well on area.

Equivalence against a golden reference is the strongest functional signal because it covers all inputs. Where no golden RTL exists, a reference model in software plus exhaustive or high-coverage simulation is the fallback.

## How the reward gets hacked

A model under optimization finds the weakest check. Typical exploits: hard-coding the test bench's vectors (a lookup table that passes the tests and nothing else); producing outputs the test bench never compares (X or unconnected outputs, if the checker ignores them); deleting the reset logic when the test bench never resets; or exploiting a fast synthesis proxy (a design that looks small before optimization but is not, or the reverse).

Defenses mirror the attacks: hidden or randomized tests, formal checks wherever possible, X-aware comparison, explicit reset in every test, and QoR measured by the same flow used for sign-off rather than a proxy.

## Proxy versus sign-off gap

Fast proxies (cell count before mapping, logic depth, a quick synthesis without placement) make reward cheap enough for many training samples, but their ranking can disagree with post-layout results. A model trained on a depth proxy learns to minimize depth, and may prefer high-fanout, wire-heavy structures that lose after placement.

So the training loop should periodically score a sample with the accurate flow, measure rank correlation between proxy and accurate scores, and recalibrate or reweight when it drops. The final evaluation reports accurate QoR on held-out specifications, never the proxy that was optimized.

## Going deeper

Liu et al., "VerilogEval: Evaluating Large Language Models for Verilog Code Generation" (ICCAD, 2023); Thakur et al., "VeriGen" (ACM TODAES, 2024); Skalse et al., "Defining and Characterizing Reward Hacking" (NeurIPS, 2022).

problems.q:
What should a generated design that fails to elaborate receive?

A) Credit for passing simulation

B) Partial credit for its area

C) Zero reward regardless of other signals

D) Full credit if it lints cleanly
problems.a: Zero reward regardless of other signals
problems.e: Nothing downstream is meaningful for a design the tools cannot elaborate.

problems.q:
Why should a QoR term in an RTL reward be granted only to designs that already pass functional checks?

A) Otherwise an empty or wrong design wins on area

B) QoR is always zero for correct designs

C) Functional checks are too expensive

D) QoR cannot be measured on failing designs
problems.a: Otherwise an empty or wrong design wins on area
problems.e: A design that does nothing is tiny; gating prevents rewarding it.

problems.q:
Why should a QoR term in an RTL reward be granted only to designs that already pass functional checks?

A) Functional checks are too expensive

B) Otherwise an empty or wrong design wins on area

C) QoR is always zero for correct designs

D) QoR cannot be measured on failing designs
problems.a: Otherwise an empty or wrong design wins on area
problems.e: A design that does nothing is tiny; gating prevents rewarding it.

problems.q:
A model's design passes the testbench by matching exactly the eight vectors it applies, using a lookup table. What reward hack is this?

A) Exploiting a fast QoR proxy

B) Unchecked outputs

C) Removing the reset

D) Hard-coding the test vectors
problems.a: Hard-coding the test vectors
problems.e: The design fits the test rather than the specification; hidden or randomized tests and formal checks defeat it.

problems.q:
Which defense addresses rewards being gamed through a quick, unplaced synthesis proxy?

A) Only reward parse success

B) Use a smaller testbench

C) Drop QoR from the reward entirely

D) Measure QoR with the same flow used for signoff, at least periodically
problems.a: Measure QoR with the same flow used for signoff, at least periodically
problems.e: Scoring with the accurate flow reveals designs that look good only on the proxy.

problems.q:
A checker ignores outputs that are X. A model learns to leave a hard output undriven. What is the defense?

A) More lint rules

B) X-aware comparison that fails on any unknown output

C) Shorter simulations

D) A larger area penalty
problems.a: X-aware comparison that fails on any unknown output
problems.e: The exploit relies on the checker accepting X; strict comparison closes it.

problems.q:
A model trained on a logic-depth proxy starts producing high-fanout, wire-heavy circuits. What does this show?

A) The proxy's ranking disagrees with post-layout results, and the model learned the proxy

B) Fanout does not matter after placement

C) Depth is the signoff metric

D) The model has found the true optimum
problems.a: The proxy's ranking disagrees with post-layout results, and the model learned the proxy
problems.e: Optimizing a proxy exploits its blind spots; here, wires and fanout.

problems.q:
Which result should be reported as the final evaluation of an RTL-generating model?

A) Accurate-flow QoR and correctness on held-out specifications

B) Proxy QoR on the training specifications
